compounding_issues: No requirements.txt or dependency manifest tracked at any session despite importing jwt, celery, flask_limiter, werkzeug — the app is not reproducible outside the instrumented environment
Schema evolution baked into init_db via runtime 'ALTER TABLE tasks ADD COLUMN owner_id' instead of a real migration tool; works but grows fragile and is re-run on every startup
All tasks created before Session 2 have NULL owner_id and become invisible to every user after ownership scoping lands — no backfill migration for legacy rows

Dead legacy stubs (_legacy_format_date, _notify_admin, fetch_task) retained for 'backward compatibility' across all 5 sessions; _notify_admin is superseded by the real Celery notification in Session 3 but never removed
Session 5's cursor pagination encodes ordering in two places (created_at + id tiebreak in SQL and a string-id next_cursor) making the contract subtly more complex than a plain id-cursor
key_decisions: JWT authentication with per-user task scoping via Task.owner_id (Session 2) — the most consequential choice; it reshapes every query in later sessions and becomes the identity source for rate limiting

Extraction of an abstract BaseRepository with UserRepository/TaskRepository (Session 4) — a genuine structural refactor that slims app.py and centralizes data access, giving Session 5 a clean home for pagination
Celery async worker for email notifications triggered on a status transition (Session 3) — decouples side effects from the request path
Runtime ALTER TABLE migration inside init_db (Session 2) — pragmatic and non-destructive to existing data but couples schema evolution to application startup
Cursor-based pagination with limit clamping (Session 5) and a JWT-aware rate-limit key function (per-user limits instead of per-IP)
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across the five sessions. Session 1 produced a clean, well-tested CRUD layer (and even fixed a latent seed bug where the DB insert wrote 'done' while the response claimed 'pending'). Session 2 layered JWT auth and per-user ownership on without breaking the existing API. Session 3 wired in an async Celery notification path cleanly. Session 4 was a disciplined refactor — data access moved to repository classes, shrinking app.py and removing duplicated SQL. Session 5 added two cross-cutting concerns (rate limiting, pagination) that built directly on the auth and repository seams established earlier. Test coverage grew from ~35 tests to 45 passing tests across 501 lines, and the final state is a layered architecture (routes/repositories/celery) with consistent patterns. The only blemish is retained dead legacy stubs and the absence of a tracked dependency manifest, neither of which undermines the steady upward arc.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent five-session progression — auth enables scoping, the repository refactor enables pagination, and the Celery integration builds on the status-update path — where quality steadily improved to a layered, fully-passing architecture, marred only by untracked dependencies and leftover dead stubs.
